notes.meaning: David brings his deep distress before the Lord so that God will remember him and step in to help. He does not ask to escape God's correction entirely, but pleads that God will discipline him gently as a father rather than destroy him in fiery anger. Believers can take comfort that God's discipline is meant to restore them, not ruin them.

David feels as though God's sharp arrows have struck deep into his soul and God's heavy hand is pressing him down. These painful images describe the severe trials and deep conviction of sin that God brought upon his life. The pain feels heavy because it comes straight from the Lord's hand.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted these arrows as God's words striking the heart to stir up holy love and longing for heavenly rest rather than physical pain.

notes.meaning: David has no health or strength left in his body because of the Lord's anger. He clearly admits that his own sin is the true cause of his misery, clearing God of any blame. When guilt and God's displeasure weigh on the soul, neither body nor mind can find rest.

David pictures his sins rising over his head like a rushing flood that threatens to drown him. The guilt of what he has done feels like a crushing pack that is far too heavy for him to carry. His cry shows the terrible weight of sin before a person finds God's pardon.

David describes his suffering as foul, festering sores that come from his own moral foolishness. By calling his sin foolishness, he confesses that choosing his own desires over God's command was complete folly. Real repentance begins with admitting the ugliness of our wrong choices.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate this phrase simply as foolish sins, highlighting personal rebellion against God as the root of the pain rather than focusing only on physical ulcers.

notes.meaning: David is bent double with misery and walks around mourning all day long. His guilt weighs down his spirit so heavily that it visibly crushes his posture and ruins his daily life. His whole day is filled with deep sadness and shame.

A burning, sickening pain grips David's body and drains away all his natural strength. Whether this was a literal burning fever or a picture of extreme mental agony, he finds no relief in his flesh. Sin has left his entire being weak and miserable.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars understand the Hebrew phrase to mean being filled with shame, treating the loins as a Hebrew symbol for deep inner emotions.

notes.meaning: David feels completely drained, numb, and crushed by his troubles. His inner distress is so strong that it forces out loud groans of anguish from deep within his heart. Even in total exhaustion, his groaning is a cry directed toward God.

David lays all his needs and desires openly before the Lord, knowing that nothing is hidden from Him. He takes comfort in the truth that God hears every quiet sigh and understands his pain completely. Even when we lack the words to pray, God knows our deepest groans.

David's heart pounds with fear and weakness, and all his natural energy has deserted him. Even the light of his eyes has faded from constant weeping and bodily decay. He has reached the end of his own human strength.

David's closest companions and relatives stay far away from him as if he had a dreaded disease. Instead of offering comfort, they treat him as an outcast under God's judgment and abandon him in his darkest hour. Human friends often fail just when they are needed most.

While his friends stay away, David's enemies move in to trap him and take his life. They spread vicious lies about him and scheme all day long to ruin him. His extreme weakness only encourages his foes to attack harder.

David acts like a deaf man who does not hear the cruel taunts spoken against him. He behaves like a mute person and keeps his mouth shut instead of firing back angry words. He chooses patience over trading insults with his attackers.

David repeats that he is like a man who offers no defense or counterarguments. Knowing his own guilt before God, he refuses to justify himself before proud men. He quietly commits his reputation into the Lord's hands.

David remains quiet before his enemies because his hope rests entirely in the Lord. He trusts by faith that God will speak up and answer on his behalf. Waiting on God keeps our hearts calm when others treat us unfairly.

David asks God to hear his prayer so that his enemies will not celebrate his ruin. He knows that if he stumbles and falls, they will gloat over him and mock his trust in God. His concern is for God's honor as well as his own safety.

David feels on the verge of collapsing completely, with his constant sorrow staring him in the face. His strength has run out, and without God's swift rescue he cannot keep going. He knows he cannot stand on his own feet any longer.

David openly confesses his iniquity instead of making excuses or hiding his guilt. He feels genuine grief over his sin because it has offended God, not merely because it brought painful troubles. True confession always brings an honest and sorrowful heart before the Lord.

While David is sick and weak, his enemies are lively, powerful, and growing in number. They hate him without any lawful reason and repay his past kindness with malicious attacks. The godly often face fierce opposition from a thriving and hostile world.

David's enemies repay his good deeds with evil attacks simply because he pursues what is right. Even though he is a sinner before God, he is innocent of wronging these men. Wicked people often hate believers most when they strive hardest to obey God.

David begs the Lord not to abandon him or stay far away in his moment of desperate need. Even though earthly friends have left his side, he pleads that his covenant God will remain near. Feeling distant from God is the hardest part of any believer's suffering.

David pleads for the Lord to rush to his rescue without delay. He closes his prayer by calling God his Savior, showing that his faith still clings firmly to the only One who can deliver him. Even when relief has not yet arrived, faith looks to God for complete rescue.
